# How to use this reference

If your question is “How many people do I recruit?”, start with the study
design below. If it is “Has anyone obtained this number independently?”,
go to the [published comparisons](#evidence). A formula, an R function and a
published numerical result are three different things. For example, the
same function that reproduces a published requirement of 326 people can also
calculate a design for which there is no published numerical benchmark.

[Getting started](paweh-01-getting-started.html) introduces power (the
probability of rejecting the null hypothesis under a specified alternative),
the significance level (the intended rejection probability under the null),
and minimum sample size (MSSN). The functions here **plan** studies. An
expected genotype count, transmission count or test statistic in a design
is not an observed association in patient data.

| What is sampled and measured? | Where to look |
|:--|:--|
| Unrelated cases and controls with called genotypes | [Case-control designs](#case-control); recruitment is cases **plus** their controls. |
| An affected child and both parents, with called genotypes | [Transmission designs](#tdt); the unit is a complete trio. |
| One or more continuous traits | [Quantitative traits](#qtl); distinguish people screened from people selected for genotyping. |
| Sequence reads at specified depth | [Sequencing](#sequencing); cases and controls are called first, whereas the trio method uses read counts directly. |
| Routine measurements plus reference assessments for a subset | [LRTae](#lrtae); the four validation groups together make up the total enrollment. |

# A reading guide to the textbook

All numbered book sections and equations below refer to Gordon, Finch and
Kim, [*Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to Assess, Address, and
Account for Mixtures in Association Studies*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-61121-7)
(2020). The book connects the methods; the papers in the last column identify
their origins or, where indicated, a related comparison. Follow the linked
tutorials for inputs and executable examples.

| Chapter and sections | What to read for; package and primary sources |
|:--|:--|
| 1. Introduction to Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics | §§1.4.1–1.4.2: obtain genotype frequencies directly or derive them from risk. §§1.6.1.1–1.6.1.3 introduce the tests; §1.6.1.4 gives design noncentrality parameters (NCPs): Eq. 1.22 for the genotype test, 1.24 for trend, 1.25 for affected-child transmissions. See [case-control](paweh-02-case-control-study-design.html) (`cc_power()`: Pearson; Cochran; Armitage) and [TDT](paweh-03-tdt-study-design.html) (`tdt_power()`: Spielman et al.; Deng and Chen). |
| 2. Overview of Genomic Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics | §2.3 gives call-error models; §2.5.2 explains differential error (Gordon et al. 2002; Moskvina et al.). §2.7.1.2, Eq. 2.16 gives the [case mixture](paweh-02-case-control-study-design.html) in `cc_mssn()`. §§2.6.1–2.6.2 describe read probabilities relevant to [sequencing](paweh-06-sequencing-study-design.html); they do not supply the package's case-control calling pipeline. |
| 3. Phenotypic Heterogeneity | §§3.3.1–3.3.2 explain how prevalence and diagnostic error change the genotype distribution among recorded cases. See Edwards et al. and [case-control power](paweh-02-case-control-study-design.html). |
| 4. Association Tests Allowing for Heterogeneity | §§4.2.1.1–4.2.1.4 give the validation tiers, observed-data likelihood, statistic and example (Gordon et al. 2004; Barral et al.). Compare Ji et al. for [prospective LRTae](paweh-07-lrtae-study-design.html), including `lrtae_ncp()`. §§4.4.2.1–4.4.2.4 develop Kim's [trio read likelihood](paweh-06-sequencing-study-design.html) used for `tdt_ngs_power()`; §4.4.1 describes a different case-control read test. |
| 5. Designing Genetic Linkage and Association Studies that Maintain Desired Statistical Power in the Presence of Mixtures | For [case-control planning](paweh-02-case-control-study-design.html), §§5.2.1–5.2.2 treat non-differential call and diagnosis errors; §5.3.1 treats locus mixtures. For [trio planning](paweh-03-tdt-study-design.html), §5.2.5 treats genotype errors and null rejection, §5.2.6 phenotype errors (Buyske et al.), §5.3.3 unlinked families (Chen et al.). §5.4.4 covers [Kim's sequencing design](paweh-06-sequencing-study-design.html). §5.2.3 studies LRTae power empirically; it is not the derivation of Ji's analytical NCP. |
| 6. Threshold-Selected Quantitative Trait Loci and Pleiotropy | §§6.1.1–6.1.3 develop genotype means and tail probabilities (Falconer and Mackay); §6.1.4 covers ANOVA. §§6.2.1–6.2.2 develop the multiple-trait model, §6.2.3 joint thresholds and §6.2.4 the multivariate test. See the [quantitative-trait tutorial](paweh-04-quantitative-trait-study-design.html) and `qtl_multivariate_mssn_full()`. Gordon et al. (2017), rather than the book's §6.2.4 example, supplies the 326-person comparison. |

# Unrelated cases and controls {#case-control}

The Pearson genotype test asks whether *any* of the three genotype proportions
differ between groups (two degrees of freedom). The Cochran–Armitage trend
test asks whether a specified genotype score differs on average (one degree
of freedom). Scores of 0, 1 and 2 target an allele-dose trend; they can miss
a strong heterozygote effect. `cc_power()` and `cc_mssn()` compare the
expected groups at a specified control-to-case ratio. Both use large-sample
approximations. The trend NCP scales the squared difference in mean scores by a
pooled score variance; the sequencing design applies it to called genotypes.

**Inputs.** With model-based inputs, population allele frequency,
Hardy–Weinberg proportions (the genotype proportions expected under random
pairing of alleles), prevalence and genotype relative risks determine the
two rows. With model-free inputs, supply the three genotype frequencies
among true cases and among true controls in the same allele order. “Model-free”
dispenses with an inheritance model; it still assumes the proposed rows
represent the planned study and that people are sampled independently.

| Change to the design | What the comparison means |
|:--|:--|
| Genotype misclassification (Gordon et al. 2002; Ahn et al. 2007) | Apply a transition matrix to each true genotype distribution. In the Douglas–Skol–Boehnke model (Gordon, Table 1b), a homozygote becomes heterozygous with probability γ; a heterozygote becomes *either* homozygote with total probability η. Set `e1` = γ and `e2` = η/2 (older notation: δ and ε/2). With γ = η = 0.10, the heterozygote row is 0.05, 0.90, 0.05. A direct switch between opposite homozygotes is excluded. |
| Differential genotype error (Moskvina et al. 2006) | Different matrices for cases and controls can make identical biological distributions look different. Rejection at a nominal cutoff may then be a false positive. The package scenario illustrates this mechanism; it does not calibrate a new cutoff or reproduce a particular Moskvina simulation. |
| Phenotype misclassification (Edwards et al. 2005) | A false negative moves a true case to the recorded controls; a false positive moves a true control to the recorded cases. Weight both contributions by population prevalence before conditioning on the recorded label. A 1% false-positive rate can seriously dilute the case group of a rare disease. |
| Locus heterogeneity (book §2.7.1.2) | Only fraction `pi` of cases has the associated distribution; the remainder has the control distribution. Controls stay fixed. This shifts both genotype and trend contrasts. It assumes a control-like background for the other cases; it does not estimate membership. |

The [case-control tutorial](paweh-02-case-control-study-design.html) shows
these as **separate** sensitivity scenarios. For the narrower interfaces,
each pair below computes fixed-sample power or solves for sample size:

| Calculation | Specialized exports |
|:--|:--|
| Genotype test, one error rate in every off-diagonal cell, including opposite homozygotes | `cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_1p()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_1p()` |
| Two adjacent-call probabilities (Douglas–Skol–Boehnke) | `cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_2p()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_2p()` |
| Three rates, allowing opposite homozygote calls | `cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_3p()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_3p()` |
| Separate three-rate matrices by disease group | `cc_chisq_power_genotype_misclassification_differential_3p()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_genotype_misclassification_differential_3p()` |
| Diagnosis error, supplied affected and unaffected genotype distributions | `cc_chisq_power_phenotype_misclassification()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_phenotype_misclassification()` |
| Locus mixture, supplied associated and control distributions | `cc_chisq_power_locus_heterogeneity()`, `cc_chisq_mssn_locus_heterogeneity()`; `cc_trend_power_locus_heterogeneity()`, `cc_trend_mssn_locus_heterogeneity()` |

The first four pairs construct the underlying groups from a genetic model.
Use the canonical interfaces for a genotype-error comparison with supplied
group frequencies. Gordon and Edwards provide numerical checks below; the
one- and three-rate sensitivity analyses are not additional replications.

# Affected children and their parents {#tdt}

The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT; Spielman, McGinnis and Ewens)
compares the two alleles that a heterozygous parent could transmit to an
affected child. In prospective planning we need expected informative
transmissions of the designated allele (ET) and expected informative
non-transmissions (ENT). Neither counts all parents. For a planned set of
independent trios, the affected-child NCP is
\((ET-ENT)^2/(ET+ENT)\) (Deng and Chen; book §1.6.1.4, Eq. 1.25).
A larger NCP moves the test statistic farther from its null distribution.

| Task in the [TDT tutorial](paweh-03-tdt-study-design.html) | Interfaces and assumptions |
|:--|:--|
| Plan a clean or modified design | `tdt_power()`, `tdt_mssn()`. Derive counts from frequency, risks, prevalence and marker–disease association, or scale externally supplied ET and ENT from a **known number of trios**. Counts alone cannot identify genotype-call errors. |
| Derive informative transmissions | `tdt_expected_transmission_probability()`, `tdt_expected_nontransmission_probability()`, `tdt_expected_transmission_counts()`. Scale per-parent probabilities across the two parents. The helpers default to `theta1 = pd`; in the underlying equations `theta1` is a recombination fraction. Set it to zero to match the canonical linked component. These defaults describe different designs. |
| Convert counts or a genetic model to a design | `tdt_power_from_expected_counts()`, `tdt_power_from_model()`, `tdt_mssn_from_model()`. These expose the ordinary count/NCP steps; they are not new association tests. |
| Allow diagnostic false positives | Buyske et al.; §5.2.6. Mix true affected-child families with families admitted by the screen. Prevalence determines the fraction of screen-positive children truly affected. `tdt_mssn_phenotype_misclassification_from_ncp()` starts with baseline NCP information. See the **relative**, not absolute, reproduction below. |
| Allow locus heterogeneity | Chen et al.; §5.3.3. Mix linked families with an unlinked component with balanced expected transmission. Here `heter_rate` is the **unlinked** fraction. The comparison below uses 0% and 50%. |

**Genotype errors are a different calculation.** In §5.2.5, especially
§5.2.5.1, errors move calls by one allele copy. The model applies independent
calls to all three family members, then conditions on calls consistent with
Mendelian inheritance. Errors that pass that check can still bias
transmission. The canonical model-based scenario extends the textbook's
null calculation to planning under association. In the tutorial illustration with 1% error per adjacent call,
the required number rises from 215 to 249 *retained* trios and the null
rejection rate at 600 trios is about 5.75% at nominal 5%. Neither number
is an empirical error correction. Use one modifier at a time; these functions
do not fit the observed-data TDTae or jointly model all three mechanisms.

# Quantitative traits and pleiotropy {#qtl}

What if disease status is not observed because the outcome is continuous?
A quantitative trait locus (QTL) shifts the distribution of a measurement.
Pleiotropy means one locus can shift several traits. The
[quantitative-trait tutorial](paweh-04-quantitative-trait-study-design.html)
compares keeping each measurement with selecting only people in the extremes.

| Design | Exports and statistical basis |
|:--|:--|
| Model the trait | `qtl_falconer_parameters()` derives genotype means and a common residual variance from the allele frequency, fraction of variance explained and dominance-to-additivity ratio. `qtl_falconer_threshold_parameters()` conditions genotype frequencies on eligibility for each tail. These are helpers for the Falconer model (Fisher; Falconer and Mackay; Lynch and Walsh; §§6.1.1–6.1.3). |
| Keep all observations | `qtl_anova_power()`, `qtl_anova_mssn()`: a one-way ANOVA compares the three genotype means using a noncentral F distribution (Scheffé; §6.1.4). The calculation assumes independent observations, Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies and common within-genotype variance; sparse groups affect the approximation. |
| Genotype extreme individuals | `qtl_threshold_chisq_power()`, `qtl_threshold_chisq_mssn()`: compare genotype frequencies in upper and lower tails using Pearson's test. Reference-normal cutoffs are applied to a **mixture** of genotype-specific normals: the realized population eligibility need not be the nominal tail fraction. Li et al. provide related extreme-sampling context. |
| Measure several traits per person | `qtl_multivariate_power_full()`, `qtl_multivariate_mssn_full()`: choose continuous Pillai MANOVA (Pillai; Gordon et al. 2017) or the joint-threshold genotype comparison (§§6.2.1–6.2.4). Supply a positive-definite **within-genotype** correlation matrix in trait order, not marginal correlations across all genotypes. |

Pillai's trace measures separation of the genotype-specific mean vectors
relative to within-group variation; its design calculation uses the mean
and covariance matrices. The threshold alternative selects people above
**every** upper cutoff or below **every** lower cutoff. For each genotype,
integrate its joint normal distribution over each corner, weight by genotype
frequency, then compare genotypes between selected groups. Multiplying
marginal tail probabilities is generally wrong for correlated traits.

paweh uses a univariate normal probability for one trait, deterministic
Miwa–Hayter–Kuriki integration for 2–20 traits and randomized Genz–Bretz
integration with a fixed local seed above 20. Inspect integration diagnostics,
especially for small joint probabilities. These choices implement the
probability calculation; neither the integration settings nor the tutorial's
joint-tail recruitment example is a published Pillai result.

# Sequencing: genotype calls or raw reads? {#sequencing}

The [sequencing tutorial](paweh-06-sequencing-study-design.html) compares
two data models. In both, depth is a fixed number of reads, not a mean over
a distribution of depths. A per-read error is not the probability of calling
the wrong genotype.

**Case-control NGS.** At depth \(v\) and symmetric per-read error \(e\),
the alternate-read count is binomial with success probability \(e\), 0.5 or
\(1-e\), given zero, one or two copies. `ngs_genotype_error_matrix()`
assigns each possible count to its maximum-likelihood genotype, with a
deterministic tie rule. Summing over counts gives a matrix with true
genotypes in rows and called genotypes in columns.
`cc_ngs_power()` and `cc_ngs_mssn()` transform each group's genotype
frequencies by its matrix, then compare mean called-genotype scores using
the Ahn/Chapman–Nam trend NCP. The **composition** is specific to paweh.
Ahn et al. start with given call-error probabilities; they did not propose
this sequencing caller. Nor is this the raw-read LTTae,NGS in book §4.4.1.

Depth and base error may differ by case status. Diagnosis error or locus
heterogeneity changes the distribution *before* sequencing; optional
additional genotype error changes calls *after* sequencing. These are
separate sensitivity scenarios. Even if the true groups are alike, different
measurement processes can create a score contrast. More apparent power in
that setting is not evidence for a biological effect.

**Family TDT1-NGS.** `tdt_ngs_power()` and `tdt_ngs_mssn()` retain
uncertain reads. Kim (2015), Appendix B, weights the read likelihood over
15 ordered, Mendelian-consistent parental and child genotype configurations.
The model uses independent trios, random mating and parental Hardy–Weinberg
frequencies, conditionally binomial reads and multiplicative risk
\(R_2=R_1^2\). The one-parameter NCP is
\(N\{\log(R_1)\}^2 I_{\mathrm{eff}}\), with per-trio information evaluated under
the null after allowing for nuisance parameters. Kim describes the benchmark effect as an odds ratio; paweh uses its
numerical value as the one-copy risk in this model. The interface allows fixed
depths by family role and directional base errors. A child with an ambiguous
genotype still contributes through the possible family configurations.

The optional false-positive diagnosis and unlinked-family scenarios multiply
Kim's sequencing NCP by the ratio of modified to baseline **ordinary TDT**
per-trio NCP coefficients (Buyske; Chen; §§5.2.6 and 5.3.3). These
calculations use prevalence, maximal positive linkage disequilibrium
(\(D'=1\)) and the bridge's \(\theta_1=p_d\) setting. Each modifier is compared
with the sequencing-only design. The ratio is a package approximation:
it does not refit the raw-read likelihood or recalculate its information
with misclassified children or unlinked families.

# Validation subsamples and LRTae {#lrtae}

Suppose everyone has routine disease and genotype measurements, but only a
subset receives a more reliable assessment. LRTae is the likelihood ratio
test allowing for error. Gordon et al. (2004) developed the double-sampling
test; Barral et al. (2006) describe fitting it to observed data. **Ji et
al. (2005)** is the source for *prospective* asymptotic power and sample
size. The [LRTae tutorial](paweh-07-lrtae-study-design.html) shows what can
be planned without fitting a single observed patient record.

| Function | What it uses and returns |
|:--|:--|
| `lrtae_ncp()` | Add expected information across four disjoint tiers: routine only, reference phenotype only, reference genotype only, both references. Remove the information shared with nuisance parameters (free case genotype frequencies and true control sampling share) by a Schur complement. The resulting quadratic form measures separation between the true case and control genotype distributions. |
| `lrtae_power()` | Given tier counts, compare the corresponding noncentral chi-square distribution to the central cutoff (two degrees of freedom for three genotypes). The input concerns a proposed alternative, not an observed likelihood ratio. |
| `lrtae_mssn()` | Given tier **shares**, find an integer total reaching target power. The Hamilton largest-remainder rule floors the four quotas and assigns remaining places in decreasing order of fractional remainder, breaking ties in tier order. This implements a specified allocation; it does not optimize the shares or cost. |

Reference assessments are treated as truth. Routine error matrices are
fixed planning inputs: a row conditions on a **true** state and sums to one
over reported states. The genotype and phenotype errors combine independently
given the true categories. If the information matrix is singular the design
cannot identify the necessary contrasts. The package does not estimate
error rates, fit the observed-data LRTae, or perform the distinct LTTae trend
test (§4.2.2).

# Plots, dashboard and related software

The figures evaluate the underlying designs over a grid or display a model
distribution. Their scientific sources are those of the corresponding rows
above; a sensitivity curve is not another published statistical test.

| Interface | What is drawn |
|:--|:--|
| `plot_cc_power()`, `plot_cc_mssn()` | Power or case recruitment as a case-control assumption changes. |
| `plot_tdt_power()`, `plot_tdt_mssn()`, `plot_tdt_surface3d()` | Power or trio recruitment over one input or a two-input grid. |
| `plot_tdt_power_phenotype_misclassification()`, `plot_tdt_mssn_phenotype_misclassification()`; `plot_tdt_power_locus_heterogeneity()`, `plot_tdt_mssn_locus_heterogeneity()` | Specialized views of the Buyske and Chen family sensitivities. |
| `plot_qtl_genotype_distribution()`, `plot_qtl_anova_power()`, `plot_qtl_anova_mssn()` | Genotype-specific trait distributions and continuous-trait design curves. |
| `plot_qtl_threshold_chisq_power()`, `plot_qtl_threshold_chisq_mssn()` | Power or recruitment among selected extremes. |
| `plot_ngs_power()`, `plot_ngs_mssn()` | Sequencing sensitivity for the chosen case-control or trio design. |
| `paweh_app()` | Opens the [interactive dashboard](paweh-05-interactive-dashboard.html). Read the unit and assumptions shown for the selected design; the app is an interface to calculations. |

Other genetic study planners address related questions.
USC's [Quanto](https://keck.usc.edu/biostatistics/software/) includes
gene–environment and gene–gene interactions. Michigan's
[CaTS](https://csg.sph.umich.edu/abecasis/CaTS/reference.html) describes
one- and two-stage association designs; its
[GAS Power Calculator](https://csg.sph.umich.edu/abecasis/gas_power_calculator/about.html)
adapts CaTS for one-stage studies. These are software references, not the
source of the equations above or independent checks of the outputs below.

# What has been reproduced? {#evidence}

The evidence attaches to a **particular output at particular inputs**.
*Exact published reproduction* means agreement at the precision actually
published; *approximate published reproduction* means close agreement with
a stated difference. *Relative-effect reproduction* means that a ratio
agrees while absolute results differ. A *published-method implementation*
has a methodological source but no established match for the particular
number. An *illustrative calculation* demonstrates a design without claiming
a published numerical target. An *unresolved comparison* identifies what
still needs independent evidence. Regression tests serve another purpose:
they detect changes to a stored software result, even when its original
source is uncertain.

| Comparison and inputs | Source, package result and evidence |
|:--|:--|
| **Case-control genotype error** — Gordon et al. (2002), Fig. 1b; equal groups, 95% power, nominal 5% | Accurate calls: about 386 cases in the paper; continuous 386.0778, hence 387 whole cases in paweh (**approximate**). With γ = η = 10%: 477 cases in both (**exact**). Add an equal number of controls in each design. |
| **Case-control phenotype error** — Edwards et al. (2005); 250 per group, nominal 1%, no false negatives | For (prevalence, false-positive rate) of (5%, 1%), (1%, 1%), (5%, 2%), (1%, 2%), the reported powers are 91%, 33%, 76%, 11%. paweh gives 91.35%, 33.20%, 76.34%, 10.98%: **exact at published whole-percent precision**. |
| **Ordinary genotype error** — Ahn et al. (2007), p. 257; 1,000 per group at nominal 0.001 | Published trend/genotype powers about 0.88/0.81 (accurate calls) and 0.79/0.70 (5% adjacent transitions); calculated 0.8743/0.8061 and 0.7876/0.6992 (**approximate**). This checks the genotype-based calculation, not the upstream depth-to-call model. |
| **Trio phenotype error** — Buyske et al. (2009), p. 291; 1% prevalence, 0% versus 5% false positives | Paper: 691 versus 27,118 trios. Package: 546 versus 21,401 whole trios. Recruitment rises about 39-fold in each (**relative effect**). The large absolute difference is **unresolved**; the corrected expressions in book §5.2.6 do not by themselves explain it. |
| **Trio locus heterogeneity** — Chen et al. (2009), Fig. 2; none versus half unlinked | Paper: 3,430 versus 13,721 trios; package: 3,431 versus 13,723. **Approximate** (one and two trios higher). The cause has not been established; do not assume rounding explains it. |
| **One quantitative trait** — book §§6.1.3–6.1.4; allele frequency 0.15, QTL variance 0.025, dominance ratio 0.5 | **Exact recruitment targets:** 996 for ANOVA on the tutorial's grid (rounded genotype counts 720, 254, 22; package power 0.80005); 126 per tail, 252 genotyped in total, for the threshold test (power 0.80167). These matches do not validate every printed intermediate quantity. |
| **Two continuous traits** — Gordon et al. (2017), pp. 205–206; 80% power at nominal \(5\times10^{-8}\) | **Exact:** the paper reports 326 people. Package power crosses 0.80 between 325 (0.79847) and 326 (0.80149). The fractional root 325.5057 is a software value. At allele frequency 0.05 the expected two-copy group is only \(326(0.05)^2=0.815\) people; a realized study may have none. |
| **Two selected traits** — tutorial's joint upper/lower tails | **Illustrative:** at 72 per group, power is 0.79606; at 73 it is 0.80563. This is a different design and parameter set from the 326-person reproduction. |
| **TDT1-NGS** — Kim (2015), Table 3 scenarios: allele frequency 0.35, per-read error 0.025, nominal \(5\times10^{-8}\) | At depths 4×/25×, all six stored values agree: **654/416** trios (90%, one-copy risk 2), **716/456** (70%, 1.8), **733/466** (10%, 1.5). Only the first pair is **exact at the whole-trio precision reported in the published abstract**. The other four match software benchmarks; comparison to the original table cells is **unresolved**. |
| **LRTae** — historical 500-person validation design | **Published-method implementation; illustrative numbers.** Tier counts 248/135/72/45 yield NCP 22.40827 and power 0.99250. With the same shares, nominal 5% and target 80%, 216 people (107/58/31/20) give 0.80219. No complete workbook or matching published prospective output was independently verified. |

# Qualifications that matter for reuse

- **A matching recruitment target does not settle a parameter discrepancy.**
  Book §6.1.3 prints 0.5 as a dominance deviation and −0.0985 as the
  zero-copy mean. Using 0.5 as the dominance-to-additivity *ratio* in
  §6.1.1 gives additive effect 0.227982, deviation 0.113991 and mean
  −0.097462. The univariate recruitment comparisons above still hold; the
  origin of the printed differences is unknown.
- **A similar observed example is not a prospective benchmark.** Book
  §4.2.1.4, pp. 138–141, supports the LRTae genotype matrix, frequencies to
  printed precision and tier counts, but uses 5% of true cases recorded as
  controls rather than the tutorial's 4%. Its statistic 24.1626 comes from
  fitting one dataset. Comparing it to the design NCP would answer the
  wrong question.
- **A test's nominal level is conditional on the measurement model.**
  Differential call errors can produce a case-control contrast under the
  biological null. Mendelian consistency does not remove all erroneous trio
  calls. Rare genotypes, selected tails and rare informative transmissions
  may also undermine large-sample approximations. Check the expected counts
  and interpretation of rejection before using a recruitment target.
- **Keep the denominator and units with every result.** Prevalence refers
  to the population, not the fraction of cases recruited. For extreme
  sampling, a quota of genotyped people is not the number screened. A
  trio count is neither a participant count nor an informative-parent count.
  None of the design calculations propagates arbitrary uncertainty in pilot
  inputs; vary plausible input values before committing to a study size.

# Methodological bibliography

## General design and case-control tests

- Gordon D, Finch SJ, Kim W (2020). [*Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-61121-7). Springer.
- Pearson K (1900). [On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440009463897). *Philosophical Magazine* 50:157–175.
- Cochran WG (1954). [Some methods for strengthening the common χ² tests](https://doi.org/10.2307/3001616). *Biometrics* 10:417–451.
- Armitage P (1955). [Tests for linear trends in proportions and frequencies](https://doi.org/10.2307/3001775). *Biometrics* 11:375–386.
